title: The Left Bank Perimeter: Cherbourg, the Sanatoriums, and the Science of Signs
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Norman Port and the House of Women

stops.name: Cherbourg, the birth in the naval port
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia
stops.campa: A son is born to Henriette Barthes in Cherbourg on the twelfth of November, in a Norman harbour town the navy garrisons. The father, Louis Barthes, is an officer of the merchant marine mobilised for the war as enseigne de vaisseau. Eleven months later he is dead in the North Sea, aboard the trawler Montaigne, sixteen days short of the boy's first birthday. Cherbourg leaves nothing on the son but a birth certificate. His mother takes him south to her own country before he can walk, and the harbour becomes a place he is from rather than a place he remembers.
suggested_refs: The Mémoire des Hommes death record for Louis Barthes, mort pour la France 27 October 1916
The statue of Barthes by Christine Larivière at Cherbourg, undated in reachable sources
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Roland Barthes', citing Mémoire des Hommes

stops.name: Bayonne, the household of women
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unknown and defaulted to 01 January; the sources give the Basque upbringing without dating the move south
stops.campa: Henriette Barthes carries her infant to Bayonne, where the Adour and the Nive meet and her own family has its ground. The boy grows up here on small money, in a house of women: his mother, an aunt, a grandmother. Her father was Louis-Gustave Binger, the explorer and colonial governor, which puts a famous name in the family and no money in it. Bayonne gives him a provincial Catholic rhythm and the sound of the Basque coast, and he will spend forty years in Paris setting both against the capital.
suggested_refs: The confluence of the Adour and the Nive at Bayonne
The Binger family connection through Henriette Barthes, née Binger

stops.name: Urt, the village on the Adour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, not attestation: no reachable source dates any childhood stay at Urt. fr.wikipedia names Urt only as the burial place; the family-house and school-holidays framing comes from secondary biography (Calvet, Samoyault), which was not reached this session. The 1918 date is a placement
stops.campa: Upriver from Bayonne, Urt sits on the Adour among maize fields. Biographical tradition puts the Barthes family house here and the boy in it through the school holidays of his childhood. Neither encyclopaedia article says so; the claim travels on the strength of the biographers alone and is carried here as tradition. What the record does hold is the other end of the circuit. In the spring of 1980 the body comes back to this village and goes into the ground beside Henriette, sixty-four years after she carried him out of Normandy.
suggested_refs: The village of Urt on the Adour, Pyrénées-Atlantiques
Louis-Jean Calvet and Tiphaine Samoyault on the Urt childhood, unreached this session

stops.name: Paris, the household moves north
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January
stops.campa: At eight the boy arrives in the capital he will read for the rest of his life. The household is his mother, himself, and a half-brother, Michel Salzedo, who will one day authorise the posthumous books; the German record describes the three of them in a Paris apartment under difficult money. Barthes will never marry and never leave his mother's table. Paris takes him as pupil, then as patient, then as professor, and finally as the most literary figure of the structuralist wing beside Lévi-Strauss, Lacan, Foucault and Deleuze.
suggested_refs: Michel Salzedo, half-brother, later authoriser of the posthumous publications

stops.name: Lycée Montaigne, the Latin and the Greek
stops.date_confidence: placement, not attestation: fr.wikipedia attests attendance at the lycée Montaigne and lists him in its alumni category, but gives no dates. The span c. 1924-1930 is inference and 1926 is its midpoint
stops.campa: The lycée Montaigne stands at 17 rue Auguste Comte, on the lip of the Luxembourg Gardens. Barthes does his early secondary years here, inside a perimeter of a few Left Bank streets that will hold almost his whole working life; he crosses the river to live almost never. The school gives him Latin and Greek. Forty years later the semiologist is still doing what the lycée taught, taking a word apart before he trusts its surface, reading a wrestling match or a plate of steak and chips the way he was drilled to read Cicero.
suggested_refs: Lycée Montaigne, 17 rue Auguste Comte, Paris 6e

stops.name: Lycée Louis-le-Grand, the baccalauréat and the blood
stops.date_confidence: 1934 attested by fr.wikipedia for both the baccalauréat and the first hemoptysis; the date of the transfer to Louis-le-Grand is given as 1930 in the research pool without a source line and is not independently attested here
stops.campa: For his last lycée years he transfers to Louis-le-Grand on the rue Saint-Jacques, facing the Sorbonne, the forcing house of the republic's intellectual class. He takes the baccalauréat in 1934. The same year he coughs blood and the doctors find a lesion of the left lung. Tuberculosis has declared itself, and it will run the next fifteen years: it interrupts his degree, cancels his teaching, keeps him out of the army, and sends him repeatedly out of Paris into mountain air, because there is no cure yet to send him anywhere else.
suggested_refs: Lycée Louis-le-Grand, rue Saint-Jacques, Paris 5e

stops.name: Sorbonne, classical letters between the relapses
stops.date_confidence: 1935 is an inferred start of study. The attested points inside this stop are each dated by year: the licence 1939, the exemption from military service 1937, the DES on Greek tragedy under Paul Mazon 1941
stops.campa: At the Sorbonne he reads classical letters in the gaps the illness leaves. The licence comes in 1939 and the DES, the diploma standing for a master's, in 1941, on Greek tragedy, under Paul Mazon. In 1937 he is exempted from compulsory military service on account of the lungs; the exemption is two years older than the war, and it is what keeps him out of the mobilisation when the war arrives. Isolation teaches him to read alone. The philology he is handed here he will later turn against its own grain.
suggested_refs: Paul Mazon, Hellenist, director of the 1941 DES thesis on Greek tragedy

stops.name: Lycée de Biarritz, the first post
stops.date_confidence: attested by year (fr.wikipedia); the posting is generally given as the single school year 1939-1940 and the month is unknown
stops.campa: His first teaching post takes him back to the Basque coast, professor now instead of pupil, standing in front of teenagers a few miles from the town where the women of his family raised him. It lasts one school year. The Atlantic is at the window and the war is coming; between them they end the posting. He construes Latin for adolescents through the autumn of 1939 and the spring of 1940, and then goes back to a Paris the Germans will occupy in June.
suggested_refs: Lycée de Biarritz, Pyrénées-Atlantiques

stops.name: Lycée Voltaire, teaching under the occupation
stops.date_confidence: attested as a range: fr.wikipedia gives 'aux lycées Voltaire et Buffon de Paris (1940-1941)' without splitting the two posts by month, so the year is firm and the month is defaulted
stops.campa: At 101 avenue de la République, in eastern Paris under German occupation, Barthes teaches at the lycée Voltaire. Occupied Paris offers nothing to a young man already coughing blood. The teaching itself leaves no mark on the record; what the record holds is that within the year he is in a sanatorium bed instead of in front of a blackboard. He is twenty-five, with a licence, a bad lung and a war, and nothing anyone would yet call a career.
suggested_refs: Lycée Voltaire, 101 avenue de la République, Paris 11e

stops.name: Lycée Buffon, the last classroom
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the 1940-1941 range on fr.wikipedia; the order of the two Paris lycées is not specified in the source and the Buffon post is placed second here by convention, not by evidence
stops.campa: The second occupation post is at 16 boulevard Pasteur in the fifteenth arrondissement. After Buffon he never teaches in a lycée again. Everything that follows runs through research institutes and foreign postings and, at the end, through the Collège de France, none of them Sorbonne bodies, none of them requiring him to keep a register or mark a class. The tuberculosis that closes this classroom door is also what opens the others: it takes him out of the ordinary career and never puts him back.
suggested_refs: Lycée Buffon, 16 boulevard Pasteur, Paris 15e

stops.name: Saint-Hilaire-du-Touvet, the plateau above Grenoble
stops.date_confidence: placement, not attestation: neither encyclopaedia article names this sanatorium. The site is standard in the secondary biographies, which were not reachable this session, and 1942 is a placement inside the attested 1934-1949 sanatorium span
stops.campa: Above the Isère valley a plateau of cure buildings faces the sun, reached by a funicular built for the purpose, because the only medicine anyone has for tuberculosis is altitude and stillness. Tradition puts Barthes here through the war years, among students taken out of their lives and set down to breathe. He reads. He writes. He learns the discipline of a body that has to be waited on. What the war takes from his generation in uniform it takes from him in a deck chair facing a mountain.
suggested_refs: The sanatorium des Étudiants de France at Saint-Hilaire-du-Touvet, Isère
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Roland Barthes' (sanatorium stays in France, undated)

stops.name: Leysin, the Swiss relapse
stops.date_confidence: the Switzerland element is attested (fr.wikipedia: sanatorium stays 'en France et en Suisse', running to 1949); the name Leysin comes from secondary biography not reached this session, and 1945 is a placement, not a date
stops.campa: Leysin hangs on a shoulder above the Rhône valley, its slopes lined with cure terraces, one of the tuberculosis capitals of Europe. Barthes is here on a relapse in the middle of the decade. The Swiss stays are in the record; the name Leysin is not, and comes from the biographers. In 1943, between the beds, he takes a certificate in grammar and philology. By 1949 the sanatorium years are over. He is thirty-four, with a diploma, a scarred lung and no profession.
suggested_refs: The cure terraces of Leysin, Vaud
The 1943 certificate in grammar and philology
sources: secondary biography, carried as tradition for the site

stops.name: Bucharest, librarian at the Institut français
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, recorded and not resolved: fr.wikipedia dates the librarian appointment to 1947, de.wikipedia gives the posting as 1948 to 1949. The research pool's '1947-1951' span is an artifact of a neighbouring sentence about eight articles published in Combat between August 1947 and September 1951
stops.campa: At 77 boulevard Dacia, Barthes takes a post as librarian and lecturer at the French Institute in Bucharest, a piece of French cultural diplomacy in a Romania not yet sealed. His mother comes with him; the Paris household simply moves east. He is past thirty and this is the first work he has done outside a classroom or a cure. How long he stays is not agreed. The French record says 1947, the German record says 1948 to 1949, and both stand rather than picking one.
suggested_refs: Institut Français de Bucarest, 77 bd. Dacia
The eight Combat articles, 1 August 1947 to 13 September 1951

stops.name: Alexandria, Greimas and the turn to linguistics
stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia gives the Alexandria teaching post as 1949 to June 1950. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from napoleon.journey.json and catherine_alexandria.journey.json
stops.campa: He teaches French at the University of Alexandria for a single academic year, in a port where classical antiquity, French colonial habit and Arab modernity lie stacked on one another. Here he meets the linguist Algirdas Julien Greimas, and the meeting turns him: away from impressionistic literary criticism, toward structural linguistics, toward a method for reading anything at all. It is the single most consequential encounter of his early career, arrived at almost by accident, in a colonial classroom in a city built in layers.
suggested_refs: Algirdas Julien Greimas at Alexandria, 1949-1950

hypatia.journey.json

stops.name: Paris, the Ministry and then the CNRS
stops.date_confidence: 1952 attested by year in both encyclopaedia articles; the CNRS grades that follow are attested by fr.wikipedia, stagiaire de recherche 1953 and attaché de recherche 1956-1960
stops.campa: Back in Paris he works at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and then settles at the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, where he spends seven years on lexicology and sociology. It is not a chair and it is not a following. It is a salary, a desk and no teaching load. From that desk he builds, essay by essay, the method that makes him famous outside the academy a decade before the academy will have him. He is thirty-seven and has published nothing that anyone has read.
suggested_refs: CNRS, section de lexicologie et sociologie, 1952-1960

stops.name: Paris, Le Degré zéro de l'écriture
stops.date_confidence: attested by year in both encyclopaedia articles; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The first book argues that writing is not a neutral instrument but a set of historically produced forms, and that a writer chooses a mode of writing the way a citizen inherits a politics. It is short, it is difficult, and it makes no money. What it establishes is the move he will make for the next twenty-seven years: treat the thing that looks natural as the thing most in need of explanation, and treat the explanation as a political act. Seuil publishes it, and will publish him until he dies.
suggested_refs: Le Degré zéro de l'écriture, Éditions du Seuil, 1953

stops.name: CNRS, Paris, the mythologies of the month
stops.date_confidence: attested as a range, 1954-1956: fr.wikipedia titles the series in Maurice Nadeau's revue Les Lettres nouvelles 'Petites mythologies du mois', which makes it monthly and corrects the research pool's 'bi-monthly'
stops.campa: Every month for three years he writes a short piece for Maurice Nadeau's revue Les Lettres nouvelles, under the running head Petites mythologies du mois. Wrestling. Soap powder. Steak and chips. The face of Garbo. Each one takes an object that French life presents as obvious and shows the history packed inside it and then hidden. He is doing at a desk in the CNRS what an ethnographer does in a village, except that the village is his own and the informants are advertisements.
stops.quote: The bourgeoisie is defined as the social class which does not want to be named.
suggested_refs: Les Lettres nouvelles, ed. Maurice Nadeau, the 'Petites mythologies du mois', 1954-1956

stops.name: Paris, Mythologies
stops.date_confidence: attested by year. Publisher corrected: Éditions du Seuil, per the BnF catalogue, not Les Lettres nouvelles as the infobox on en.wikipedia's 'Mythologies (book)' has it
stops.campa: Fifty-three of the short pieces are gathered by Éditions du Seuil and closed with a long theoretical essay, Le Mythe, aujourd'hui, which explains the machine the other fifty-three have been running. Myth, in the argument, is a second-order sign: it takes a history and hands it back as nature. The book sells to people who have never opened a linguistics text, and it travels. Victoria Ocampo's revue Sur is already ferrying French letters to Buenos Aires; English readers wait fifteen years and then get a version with twenty-five essays cut out.
suggested_refs: Mythologies, Éditions du Seuil, 1957
The abridged Lavers translation, 1972; the complete Howard translation, 2012
victoria_ocampo.journey.json

stops.name: Middlebury College, the summer session in Vermont
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, adjudicated and recorded: en.wikipedia gives 1957, citing Richard Howard's memoir of 1982; fr.wikipedia gives 1958. Howard's first-hand account, and the 1957 publication of the book Barthes was carrying, decide it for 1957, and fr.wikipedia's dissent is kept on the record rather than deleted
stops.campa: Barthes crosses the Atlantic for the first time to teach a summer session at Middlebury, a wooded Vermont campus whose French school teaches in French. It does not go well. He has no English to speak of and his students are not used to a visitor who has none. He arrives carrying fresh copies of a book published that spring in Paris, which nobody in Vermont has heard of. The French record dates this to 1958; his American friend, writing in 1982, dates it to 1957.
stops.quote: Myth deprives the object of which it speaks of all history. In it, history evaporates.
suggested_refs: Richard Howard, 'Remembering Roland Barthes', The Nation, 20 November 1982

stops.name: New York, Richard Howard opens the door
stops.date_confidence: summer 1957 per Richard Howard, 'Remembering Roland Barthes', The Nation, 20 November 1982, quoted on en.wikipedia; fr.wikipedia dates the New York meeting to 1959. The month is set to July from Howard's phrase 'the summer of that year'
stops.campa: Mutual friends give Barthes an address in New York. He turns up at the door of the poet Richard Howard, disconcerted by his Vermont classes, holding a fresh-printed copy of Mythologies by way of introduction. Howard will translate him for the rest of both their lives: A Lover's Discourse, Camera Lucida, the Mourning Diary, and at last the complete Mythologies in 2012, thirty-two years after Barthes is dead. Most English readers will only ever meet Barthes in Richard Howard's voice.
suggested_refs: Richard Howard, translator of Barthes into English
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Roland Barthes', quoting Howard in The Nation, 1982

stops.name: École pratique des hautes études, directeur d'études
stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia's lead gives EPHE until 1975, then EHESS, then the Collège de France. The research pool's single '1962-1980' posting wrongly ran the EPHE to his death and is corrected here
stops.campa: The EPHE has no degrees to defend and no faculty to placate, which is why the Paris structuralists collect there, Lévi-Strauss among them. Barthes is made directeur d'études and holds the seminar for thirteen years. Here the method hardens into a vocabulary: signifier and signified, denotation and connotation, the sign as a two-sided thing that language cuts out of a continuum. He is teaching, in a school outside the university, a science of meaning for which the university has no chair.
stops.quote: language is the domain of articulations, and the meaning is above all a cutting-out of shapes
stops.quote_source: Elements of Semiology, trans. Annette Lavers and Colin Smith (Hill and Wang, 1968)
suggested_refs: EPHE, sixth section, sciences économiques et sociales
The 1975 transfer to the EHESS
sources: Elements of Semiology, full text at marxists.org

stops.name: Paris, Sur Racine and the quarrel with Picard
stops.date_confidence: attested by year (fr.wikipedia); month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The structuralist reading of Racine sets off the loudest fight in French criticism since the seventeenth century's own quarrel of the ancients and the moderns. Raymond Picard of the Sorbonne answers for the profession: this is not scholarship, it is imposture. Barthes answers that the profession's own neutrality is a doctrine with a history. The row makes him a public name and a public target in the same season, and the charge follows him abroad, wherever he reads a classic against its custodians.
stops.quote: never has one brilliant writer so thoroughly misunderstood another.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Gordon, translator and editor of Voltaire's Candide, on Barthes's essay 'The Last Happy Writer'
suggested_refs: Raymond Picard, Nouvelle critique ou nouvelle imposture (1965)
Barthes, Critique et vérité (1966)

stops.name: Paris, Éléments de sémiologie
stops.date_confidence: both circulating dates are correct, for different objects: the text appears in the journal Communications no. 4 in 1964 and as a Seuil volume in 1965. en.wikipedia dates the first, fr.wikipedia the second. The research pool logged this as an unresolved conflict, which it is not
stops.campa: Saussure had proposed a general science of signs and left it unbuilt. Barthes builds a working version in eighty pages: signifier and signified, langue and parole, syntagm and system, denotation and connotation, applied not to language but to clothes, food, furniture, cars. The text runs first in the journal Communications and then as a Seuil volume the following year, which is why two dates circulate for one work. Everything he does afterwards is an application of this grid or a revolt against it.
stops.quote: there is a tendency to interpret sign as signifier, whereas this is a two-sided Janus-like entity
stops.quote_source: Elements of Semiology, trans. Annette Lavers and Colin Smith (Hill and Wang, 1968)
suggested_refs: Communications no. 4 (1964)
Éléments de sémiologie, Éditions du Seuil, 1965
sources: Elements of Semiology, full text at marxists.org

stops.name: Institut franco-japonais, Tokyo, the seminar on narrative
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by fr.wikipedia, 'L'Empire des signes'; the day is unknown and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: At fifty he leaves the West for the first time. Maurice Pinguet, director of the Institut franco-japonais at Ichigaya, invites him to lead a seminar on the structural analysis of narrative. What he finds, or rather what he builds out of what he finds, becomes L'Empire des signes four years later: chopsticks, bowing, the wrapped gift, the haiku, a city with no street names, read as a system of signs that refuse to deliver a meaning. He says plainly that it is not a book about Japan.
suggested_refs: Maurice Pinguet (1929-1991), director of the Institut franco-japonais de Tokyo
Note: the Maison franco-japonaise, 35.6441/139.7157, is a different institution and must not be conflated with this one

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, the structuralism colloquium
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day-range: the colloquium runs 18 to 21 October 1966 (en.wikipedia, 'Structure, Sign, and Play'). The research pool tagged this a reconstruction for want of a source; it is attested and has been upgraded
stops.campa: René Girard and Richard Macksey convene The Languages of Criticism and the Sciences of Man at the new Humanities Center, on Ford Foundation money, to introduce French structuralism to American academia. Barthes is in the room with Paul de Man, Jean Hyppolite and Jacques Lacan, who twenty-eight years earlier pronounced at Sainte-Anne on the incurability of Antonin Artaud. Derrida reads a paper that takes structuralism apart while the Americans are still learning its name. Foucault does not come.
suggested_refs: The Languages of Criticism and the Sciences of Man, Johns Hopkins, 18-21 October 1966
Derrida, 'Structure, Sign, and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences'
artaud.journey.json, Lacan at Sainte-Anne, 1938

stops.name: New York, The Death of the Author printed in Aspen
stops.date_confidence: attested by year (fr.wikipedia). Place corrected: the essay is published first in English, in Aspen Magazine no. 5/6, 1967, and only in 1968 in French, in no. 5 of the Marseille review Mantéia. The research pool placed the 1967 publication in Paris, which is wrong
stops.campa: The most quoted thing he ever writes appears first in English, in an American magazine that comes packed in a box rather than bound: Aspen, issue five and six. The argument is that a text is not a message from a person but a tissue of quotations, and that to hand it an author is to close it. The French text waits until 1968 and comes out of Marseille, in the fifth number of Mantéia. A theory of the vanishing author is first published in a country where the author is not yet known.
suggested_refs: Aspen Magazine no. 5/6 (1967), 'The Death of the Author'
Mantéia no. 5 (1968), Marseille, 'La Mort de l'auteur'

stops.name: Paris, Système de la mode
stops.date_confidence: attested by year (fr.wikipedia); month and day defaulted. Published in the same year as 'The Death of the Author', with no source establishing which came first
stops.campa: The doctoral-scale book takes the grid of the Éléments and lays it over the fashion press: not clothes, but the written descriptions of clothes in magazines, which is where clothing becomes a language. It is the most rigorous thing he produces and, by his own account, the least alive. He finishes it feeling the method has run out. Published in the year of the essay that kills the author, it is the last work of the systematic Barthes. What follows is pleasure, fragment and the first person.
suggested_refs: Système de la mode, Éditions du Seuil, 1967

stops.name: Rabat, teaching at the edge of the Maghreb
stops.date_confidence: attested as a range, 1969-1970 (fr.wikipedia); month and day unknown. Gap: no reachable source names the institution or the address in Rabat
stops.campa: He teaches two years in Morocco. This is not the young lecturer of Bucharest and Alexandria; this is a man in his fifties who has written Mythologies and Système de la mode and buried the author. Which building in Rabat held his classes, no reachable source says, and the absence stands rather than being filled. He arrives already the most cited literary theorist in France, teaching in a country he will not write about, in a language that is not the one being reinvented in his Paris seminars that same decade.
suggested_refs: Gap: the Rabat institution and address are unattested in reachable sources
maimonides.journey.json, Fez under the Almohads, from 1160

stops.name: Paris, S/Z and the empire of signs
stops.date_confidence: attested by year for both books in both encyclopaedia articles; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Two books in one year. S/Z takes a Balzac novella, Sarrasine, and reads it across a whole volume, cutting it into small units and sorting the codes that run through them, until the classic text stops being a story and becomes a machine seen in section. L'Empire des signes comes out of the 1966 Tokyo journey, made of photographs and short pieces about a country he says he has invented. The first is the most extreme structural reading he ever performs. The second abandons analysis. He lets the contradiction stand.
suggested_refs: S/Z, Éditions du Seuil, 1970
L'Empire des signes, Skira, 1970

stops.name: University of Geneva, the visiting chair in Saussure's city
stops.date_confidence: attested by year in both encyclopaedia articles; month and day defaulted. Coordinate note: the research pool supplied two different Geneva pins, 46.2044/6.1432 and 46.1955/6.1432, the divergence was not resolved in verification, and the first is used here
stops.campa: He holds a visiting chair in the city where Ferdinand de Saussure taught the course in general linguistics that his students published after his death, the book from which the whole science of signs descends. Barthes has spent twenty years extending Saussure to wrestling, soap, cars, photographs and dresses. No source remarks on the circuit closing; the map does it without help. The same year he publishes From Work to Text, which quietly retires the object his own method was built to dissect.
stops.quote: The Text is plural. Which is not simply to say that it has several meanings, but that it accomplishes the very plural of meaning: an irreducible (and not merely an acceptable) plural.
stops.quote_source: 'From Work to Text' (1971), trans. Stephen Heath, in Image-Music-Text, Proposition 4
suggested_refs: Saussure's Cours de linguistique générale, Geneva, published posthumously 1916

stops.name: Paris, Le Plaisir du texte
stops.date_confidence: attested by year (en.wikipedia); month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The short book abandons the science and defends the reader's body: pleasure, which the culture can accommodate, and bliss, which breaks the reader's footing and cannot. It is written in fragments, alphabetically arranged, refusing the argument shape he has used since 1953. The systematic Barthes has become the Barthes of the fragment, and the fragment is not a stylistic preference; it is the only form he can find that does not repeat itself into an institution. He is fifty-eight and famous.
stops.quote: Encratic language (the language produced and spread under the protection of power) is statutorily a language of repetition; all official institutions of language are repeating machines.
stops.quote_source: The Pleasure of the Text, trans. Richard Miller
suggested_refs: Le Plaisir du texte, Éditions du Seuil, 1973

stops.name: Beijing, the Tel Quel delegation
stops.date_confidence: attested by year; month and day unknown. Gap: no reachable source confirms cities beyond Beijing, so the itinerary is left as a gap and the journey carries a single Chinese pin
stops.campa: He goes to China with the Tel Quel group, Julia Kristeva and Philippe Sollers among the party, in the last years of the Cultural Revolution, on a chaperoned tour. Nothing comes of it. There is no Chinese Empire of Signs; the notebooks stay in a drawer until 2012. What he records is a blankness, a country whose signs will not open under the conditions of the visit. He had gone to Japan and invented a country. He goes to China and finds one that will not be invented.
stops.quote: has contrived, amazingly, to bestow an entirely new dignity upon the age-old activity, so long unjustly disparaged, of saying nothing at great length.
stops.quote_source: Simon Leys, review of Barthes's Carnets du voyage en Chine (about Barthes, not by him)
suggested_refs: Carnets du voyage en Chine, published 2012; Travels in China in English

stops.name: Paris, Roland Barthes par Roland Barthes
stops.date_confidence: attested by year in both encyclopaedia articles; the same year ends his direction of studies at the EPHE and begins the EHESS affiliation
stops.campa: Asked to write a volume about himself for a series on writers, he writes about himself in the third person, in fragments, opening with a note in his own hand saying that all of it should be considered as spoken by a character in a novel. Photographs of his mother, of Bayonne, of the Basque country fill the first pages. The author he declared dead in 1967 comes back as a fictional person. He is sixty, and he is writing about himself the way he once wrote about steak and chips.
suggested_refs: Roland Barthes par Roland Barthes, Écrivains de toujours, Éditions du Seuil, 1975

segments.name: The Mother, the Chair, the Van

stops.name: Paris, Fragments d'un discours amoureux
stops.date_confidence: attested by year in both encyclopaedia articles; month and day defaulted, and the order against the January inaugural lecture is not established by any source
stops.campa: Figures of the lover's condition, arranged alphabetically so that no argument can be built out of them: waiting, jealousy, the unbearable, the ravishment. He writes them out of his seminar. The book sells in numbers no work of literary theory sells in, to readers who have never heard of a signifier and who take it for what it is, a book about being in love. The most technical mind in French criticism has produced the year's popular success by cataloguing what everyone knows and nobody had written down.
stops.quote: Language is a skin: I rub my language against the other. It is as if I had words instead of fingers, or fingers at the tip of my words. My language trembles with desire.
stops.quote_source: A Lover's Discourse: Fragments (1977), trans. Richard Howard, section 'Talking'
suggested_refs: Fragments d'un discours amoureux, Éditions du Seuil, 1977

stops.name: Collège de France, the inaugural lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the lecture, published as Leçon. Note the correction: the election is 1976, not 1977. fr.wikipedia catalogues the first course, Comment vivre ensemble, as 'cours et séminaires au Collège de France 1976-1977', and gives the chair itself as 1977-1980. The research pool had him elected in 1977 and lecturing 'that January', which cannot both hold
stops.campa: A chair of literary semiology is created for him at the Collège de France, an institution with no degrees, no examinations and no enrolment, where the lectures are open to anyone who walks in off the street. He is elected in 1976 and gives the inaugural lecture on the seventh of January. In it he says that language is fascist, and explains that he means not that it forbids speech but that it compels one to speak inside its terms. The man who worked forty years off-centre is now standing at the centre.
suggested_refs: Leçon, the inaugural lecture of 7 January 1977
Comment vivre ensemble, cours et séminaires 1976-1977
La Préparation du roman, the final courses

stops.name: Rue Servandoni, the death of Henriette Barthes
stops.date_confidence: date attested to the day by fr.wikipedia, with en.wikipedia corroborating the year and her age of 85. The rue Servandoni address itself is a reconstruction: it comes from secondary biography not reached this session, and no encyclopaedia article names the street
stops.campa: His mother dies on the twenty-fifth of October, at eighty-five, after sixty years of the two of them keeping one household. He begins the notes the next day and keeps them for nearly two years; they are published thirty-two years later as Journal de deuil. He does not recover. Everything he writes in the three years left to him, the photography book above all, is written across this date, and the icon he hangs where her headboard stood is not hung out of faith.
stops.quote: Do not say mourning. It's too psychoanalytic. I'm not in mourning. I'm suffering.
suggested_refs: The rue Servandoni apartment behind Saint-Sulpice, Paris 6e, attested only in secondary biography

stops.name: Paris, the pastiche and the walk-on part
stops.date_confidence: 1978 attested by year for Le Roland Barthes sans peine (fr.wikipedia); the film role in Les Soeurs Brontë is attested for 1979 (en.wikipedia) and is folded into this stop rather than given a pin of its own
stops.campa: He has become famous enough to be parodied at book length: Le Roland Barthes sans peine, a satire in the form of a phrasebook for learning to speak him. The following year he takes a small part in a French film about the Brontë sisters, playing William Makepeace Thackeray. The theorist of the sign has turned into one, a recognisable manner and a vocabulary anyone can imitate and a face that can be cast. He is inside the celebrity machinery he spent the fifties taking apart in a monthly column.
suggested_refs: Le Roland Barthes sans peine (1978)
Les Soeurs Brontë (1979), dir. André Téchiné

stops.name: Paris, La Chambre claire
stops.date_confidence: attested by year, published by Seuil roughly two months before his death; the exact publication day is not given in reachable sources
stops.campa: The last book is about photography and it is about his mother. He looks for her in the family photographs and finds her in only one, taken in a winter garden when she was five, a photograph he describes at length and refuses to reproduce. Out of it he pulls the two terms that outlive him: the studium, what a picture is about, and the punctum, the detail that pierces. The argument is that a photograph certifies that a thing has been. That is what he wants from it, and it is not enough.
stops.quote: The (awesome but not painful) idea that she had not been everything to me. Otherwise I would never have written a work.
suggested_refs: La Chambre claire, Cahiers du cinéma / Gallimard / Seuil, 1980
Camera Lucida, trans. Richard Howard, Hill and Wang, 1981

stops.name: Rue des Écoles, the laundry van
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: both encyclopaedia articles agree on the date, the street and the laundry van, and fr.wikipedia gives the direction of travel as toward the Collège de France. The Mitterrand lunch is a reconstruction: it is not in fr.wikipedia's article on Barthes but in its article on Laurent Binet's novel, and the research pool cited it to the wrong page
stops.campa: On the afternoon of the twenty-fifth of February he crosses the rue des Écoles on his way to the Collège de France, a stretch between the Sorbonne and his own lecture hall that he has walked for years, and is knocked down by the van of a laundry firm. Tradition, and a novel, put a lunch with François Mitterrand an hour earlier; the encyclopaedia article on Barthes does not, and the lunch and the citation stay separate. He goes to hospital with lungs scarred since 1934.
suggested_refs: Rue des Écoles, Paris 5e, between the Sorbonne and the Collège de France
The Mitterrand lunch, attested only downstream of Binet's novel

stops.name: Pitié-Salpêtrière, the death of Roland Barthes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by both encyclopaedia articles. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from freud.journey.json, which pins La Salpêtrière at 48.8382/2.3661; the research pool supplied three mutually inconsistent pins for the hospital
stops.campa: He dies on the twenty-sixth of March, a month after the collision, of pulmonary complications on lungs the tuberculosis ruined half a century earlier. He is sixty-four. The hospital is the Pitié-Salpêtrière, where in the winter of 1885 a young Viennese doctor named Sigmund Freud stood in Charcot's wards watching hysterics and learning that a symptom could be read. Ninety-five years apart, at one address, the two ends of a century that decided everything human could be read as a text.
suggested_refs: freud.journey.json, Charcot's clinic at La Salpêtrière, winter 1885

stops.name: Urt cemetery, the grave beside his mother
stops.date_confidence: gap: no reachable source gives the date of the burial, only the year and the place (fr.wikipedia, citing Dominique Noguez in Libération). Month and day are defaulted to 01 January rather than invented for late March; the burial in fact follows the death of 26 March
stops.campa: He is not buried in Paris, where he worked for fifty-six years, and not at Père Lachaise among the philosophers. He goes back to the Basque country, to the small cemetery at Urt on the Adour, and into the ground beside Henriette. The circuit closes on itself: born in a Norman naval port to a father he never met, raised in Bayonne by the mother he never left, working his whole adult life inside a few Left Bank streets, buried in a village his readers have no reason to have heard of.
suggested_refs: Cimetière d'Urt, Chemin du Cimetière, Pyrénées-Atlantiques
Dominique Noguez in Libération, cited by fr.wikipedia for the burial

stops.name: Rue Roland-Barthes, Paris, the street named
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: fr.wikipedia, 'Rue Roland-Barthes', municipal decree of 27 November 1997. The research pool placed the street in the Bibliothèque nationale district, which is the 13th arrondissement, and gave a pin wrong by about 1.17 km
stops.campa: Seventeen years after the van, the city gives him a street: a short new way in the quartier des Quinze-Vingts in the twelfth arrondissement, cut out of the ZAC Chalon development behind the Gare de Lyon, named by municipal decree on the twenty-seventh of November. It is nowhere near the Left Bank perimeter he actually lived in. A man who spent his working life showing that a name fixes a thing and hides its history is given a nameplate on a street he never walked.
suggested_refs: Rue Roland-Barthes, quartier des Quinze-Vingts, Paris 12e, ZAC Chalon

stops.name: Paris, Journal de deuil
stops.date_confidence: attested by year of publication; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Seuil publishes the mourning notes, thirty-two years after the first of them and twenty-nine after his death, edited from the loose sheets he left behind. They are not an argument and were never meant to be read. They are the shortest sentences he ever wrote. Richard Howard translates them, as he translated almost everything else. The theorist who called the author a tissue of quotations leaves the least literary and most unguarded document of his life, and it needs no glossary.
stops.quote: In the corner of my room where she had been bedridden, where she had died and where I now sleep, in the wall where her headboard had stood against I hung an icon—not out of faith.
suggested_refs: Journal de deuil, Éditions du Seuil, 2009
Incidents, ed. François Wahl, 1987, not given a stop in this file
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Roland Barthes', citing the French publication record

stops.name: Rue des Écoles, the novel that rewrites the accident
stops.date_confidence: attested by year of publication; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Laurent Binet publishes La Septième Fonction du langage, a detective novel in which the laundry van is an assassination and the motive is a stolen page describing a seventh function of language that lets its holder do anything with words. The plot runs from the rue des Écoles through Bologna to Venice with the whole Paris intelligentsia in it as characters. Binet is why most people now know about the lunch with Mitterrand, and no encyclopaedia article is where they learned it.
suggested_refs: Laurent Binet, La Septième Fonction du langage (Grasset, 2015)
Gap flagged: attested fact and literary embellishment are not cleanly separable in the accident's afterlife
